what_it_does: Multiplying a sparse matrix (a grid of numbers where most entries are zero) by a vector is a fundamental operation in scientific simulation and graph computing, but it is notoriously hard to accelerate on GPUs because different rows of the matrix have wildly different numbers of non-zero entries and benefit from different algorithms. Today, the CPU decides which algorithm to use for each row before handing work to the GPU — an expensive round-trip that adds latency and hurts cache reuse. This paper uses 'GPU Work Graphs,' a new programming model borrowed from graphics rendering, to let the GPU schedule its own work on-the-fly as it processes rows: preprocessing and computation are interleaved on the device, each row's algorithm is selected and dispatched in hardware without involving the CPU, and the working data stays hot in the GPU's caches. The result is a fully device-driven pipeline that eliminates CPU-GPU synchronization entirely.
